name: Puyuma
confidence_why: 8 independent first-hand sources agree (5 agree, 2 refine), none contradicts

new_statements.quote: 在知本卑南語中，重音固定落在詞的倒數第一音節。加了後綴的詞亦適用此一重音規則，例如ka.rátr「咬」原本重音落在/rátr/，加上後綴-aw後變成karatráw後，重音往後移。
new_statements.translation: In Katipul (Zhiben) Puyuma, stress falls fixedly on the last syllable of the word. Words with a suffix added also follow this stress rule; for example ka.rátr 'bite' originally has its stress on /rátr/, and after the suffix -aw is added, giving karatráw, the stress moves rightward.
new_statements.citation: Deng, Fangqing [Stacy F. Teng]. 2018. 卑南語語法概論 Beinan yu yufa gailun [An introduction to Puyuma grammar] (臺灣南島語言叢書 13), 2nd ed. New Taipei: Council of Indigenous Peoples. xviii+190 pp.

Reading fixed: final syllable is right ('重音固定落在詞的倒數第一音節' = stress fixed on the last syllable, suffixed words included); no secondary stress, no exceptions. Relation 'agrees' with catalog final stress is righ…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog final stress (final syllable). Describes the Katipul/知本 dialect specifically.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word; suffixes count as part of the word, so the stress moves to the new final syllable after suffixation.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in §2.3.3; §2.3.4 (p. 13) only notes that some vowel changes depend on stressed vs unstressed position.
new_statements.identity_note: Teng 2008 describes the Nanwang (Puyuma proper) dialect of Taitung City; Deng/Teng 2018 explicitly describes 知本卑南語 (Katipul/Zhiben Puyuma), the other main dialect group. Both give final stress, so the placement holds across the two dialect groups. Cauquelin 1991 is, per Teng 2008, a sketch of the Nanwang dialect (not opened).

new_statements.quote: Word stress in Puyuma falls on the last syllable, and is thus non-phonemic. Puyuma word stress is mainly marked by greater intensity, a higher pitch level, and longer duration. [p. 22] ... An affix counts as part of the word in stress assignment, but a clitic does not. Because stress is word-final, stress is diagnostic only for suffixes and enclitics. ... When an enclitic element is attached to a host, the default is that stress falls on the host [p. 24] ... 2.4.2 Stress shift in interrogative sentences. The stress of the final word in an interrogative sentence is shifted from the last syllable to the penultimate syllable. [p. 24]
new_statements.citation: Teng, Stacy Fang-Ching (2008). A reference grammar of Puyuma. Pacific Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: §2.4 Word stress, §2.4.1 General rule for stress assignment, pp. 22-24; also fn. 18 p. 76, p. 120 (§6), §12.3.1.2 p. 222
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text layer of the PDF held by the project). Every piece of the stitched quotation is present verbatim: 'Word stress in Puyuma falls on the last syllable, and is thus non-phonemic. Puyuma word stress is mainly marked by greater intensity, a higher pitch level, and longer duration.' (§2.4.1, p. 22, the text layer); 'An affix counts as part of the word in stress assignment, but a clitic does not. Because stress is word-final, stress is diagnostic only for suffixes and enclitics.' and 'When an enclitic element is attached to a host, the default is that stress falls on the host' (p. 24, lines 1602-1608, with beray -> tu=beray-ay [tubərajáj], inaba -> inaba=ku [inabáku]); '2.4.2…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (final syllable), and adds that stress is non-phonemic, that the domain is the morphological word excluding clitics, and the three exceptions/shifts above. Describes the Nanwang dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the last syllable of the morphological word (affixes included, clitics excluded) and is non-phonemic; it is cued by intensity, higher pitch and longer duration. Enclitics attach to a stressed host without shifting stress, unless the clitic itself is focused (p. 30, §2.7).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Interrogative shift: in neutral yes/no questions the final word's stress moves from the last to the penultimate syllable, with a rise-before-fall pitch pattern (§2.4.2 p. 24; §12.3.1.2 p. 222). (2) adri.. =driya read as 'never' shifts the main verb's stress from final to penult, contrasting with 'not yet' (p. 120: t<em>alám 'not yet' vs t<em>álam 'never'). (3) The word ela 'rashly' is stressed on the first syllable, 'unlike most words, whose stress falls on the final position' (fn. 18, p. 76). Nanwang dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Teng 2008 describes the Nanwang (Puyuma proper) dialect of Taitung City; Deng/Teng 2018 explicitly describes 知本卑南語 (Katipul/Zhiben Puyuma), the other main dialect group. Both give final stress, so the placement holds across the two dialect groups. Cauquelin 1991 is, per Teng 2008, a sketch of the Nanwang dialect (not opened).

new_statements.quote: 7. Stress Stress is always on the last syllable, and has no phonological value. But vocalic length with expressive value is found in the penultimate syllable. This syllable may be very long in speech to indicate distance in time or space or for the sake of emphasis. Examples: yesterday - /adaman/ ... day before yesterday - /ada.man/ ... past - /ada ....man/ ... here - /kadiu/ there - /kadi.u/ further away - /kadi ....u/ Sometimes the emphasis is several seconds long.
new_statements.citation: Cauquelin, Josiane. 1991. The Puyuma language. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 147(1): 17-60.
new_statements.locator: Section 7 'Stress', printed p. 33 (PDF p. 18 of the KITLV/Brill open-access file)

The prose sentences are verbatim; the only…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (our earlier survey-2026-08-31) codes Puyuma as fixed final stress (final stress); Cauquelin states stress is always on the last syllable and non-phonemic, which is the same placement. It adds the expressive penultimate lengthening detail, and is consistent with Teng 2008 (final stress, non-phonemic) already recorded in this folder's.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls invariably on the final syllable and is not contrastive (no phonological value). Separately, the penultimate vowel can be expressively lengthened (sometimes for seconds) to signal temporal/spatial distance or emphasis; this is length, not a stress shift.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. The only prosodic addition is expressive (iconic) vowel lengthening of the penultimate syllable (adaman 'yesterday' vs ada.man 'day before yesterday' vs ada..man 'past'; kadiu 'here' / kadi.u 'there' / kadi..u 'further away'). No mention of interrogative penult shift or clitic behaviour (those are in Teng 2008, already logged).
new_statements.identity_note: Cauquelin 1991 explicitly describes only the Nanwang dialect of Puyuma ('In the present paper, I shall deal only with the Nanwang dialect', p. 17), as opposed to the Katipol dialect (Rikabung etc., described by Tsuchida 1980). Teng 2008, already held by the project, is also Nanwang Puyuma.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant final stress, not strict) rests on the standard English reference grammar (Teng 2008, PL-595), whose dedicated stress section with pitch/intensity figures states final, non-phonemic word stress, suffixes inside and enclitics outside the stress domain, and a penult shift only on the last word of neutral yes/no questions plus a lexical exception (ela). The quotation was verified verbatim at the cited section in the freshly downloaded open ANU PDF (previously not yet obtained locally; we have no copy and grade/quote fields empty in the record). No better or contradicting source exists in Glottolog's 13 descriptive refs or in web search (no JIPA illustration, no prosody article).
